title: Silence, poverty of speech, and the daunting subject
english: Silence is an excellent thing—for many others, most of the time, but for me now especially, since I keep my mouth shut whether I want to or not, and I am forced to be silent. I am untrained and completely unskilled in those elegant and adorned speeches that are delivered or composed with carefully chosen and approved names and words, in one continuous and unbroken flow. Perhaps I was simply not equipped by nature to produce this charming and truly Greek work. But it is now the eighth year since I myself have delivered any speech, short or long, or written anything, or heard anyone else—whether writing privately or composing history, or publicly declaiming panegyrics and debates—except for these admirable men who have embraced the noble philosophy. They care less about style and elegance of words; setting words aside, they want to investigate and state each thing accurately as it really is. Not that they reject the other thing, I think; indeed, they want as much as possible to express their excellent and accurate thoughts in excellent language free from all falsehood. But perhaps they cannot, and it is not so readily available to them: on the one hand, to unfold the sacred and divine faculty in their own words; on the other, to produce speech adorned and polished with words; and to grasp in one and the same small human mind what is the special prerogative of two separate men—especially since the method of each is different and entirely opposed. For silence is in some way friendly to thought and the discovery of things, and a partner in the work; but you would not find the faculty of speaking and dignity of delivery anywhere except in words, and in constant meditation on and use of words. And yet another discipline also violently occupies my mind and completely binds my mouth and tongue, if I should wish to say even a little in the Greek tongue: I mean our wonderful laws, by which the affairs of all who now obey the Roman empire are governed. These are not established or understood without labor and difficulty. They are wise, pious, varied, and admirable—and to sum it up in one word, most Greek. But they are set forth and handed down in the Roman language, which is certainly admirable and magnificent, and suited to the majesty of the empire, but nonetheless heavy and difficult for me. I would never say that I could feel, or be able, or wish otherwise. And since our words are nothing other than certain images of the concepts and notions of our mind, it must be confessed that those who are strong in the faculty of speaking—like certain painters, most skilled in their art and abundantly supplied with colors—can paint not only likenesses but varied ones, made most beautiful by the frequent admixture of flowers, without any hindrance.

But we, like poor men lacking such varied dyes—who either never had them in our art, or perhaps threw them away—paint and fashion the first perceptions of our mind with the words that remain, as if with only charcoal or potsherds, using common names and words. We try to represent the characters of the impressions of the mind in whatever way we can—not clearly, nor adorned for appearance, but as usually happens in charcoal painting. If anything charming and eloquent offers itself, we reject it of our own accord, as people who despise such things. But there is yet a third thing that hinders and calls me away, and much more than the others holds me back and commands me to use silence: the subject itself. I had been eager to speak about it, but now I am forced to hesitate, and I am stuck. For I have set out to speak about a man who seems to be human, and appears so; but to those who can perceive the greatness of his character and habits, he seems endowed with greater and almost divine ornaments.

orientation: Gregory is opening his address to Origen by explaining why he has been silent for eight years and why he now hesitates to speak.

title: Not his birth or body, but the godlike part of the man
english: It is not his family, nor the upbringing of his body, that I have come to praise, and so hang back and delay out of excessive scruple; nor his strength or his beauty. These are the praises given to young men, and it matters little whether they are spoken worthily or not. For to make a speech about things that neither last nor stand firm, but perish quickly and in many ways, and to do it with solemn airs and a show of dignity, and with such delays, might well prove frigid or overdone. If I had set out to speak of any of these things, I would not do it that way, since they are useless and vain, and I would never willingly have chosen to speak of them. Even so, had I set out to speak of anything of that kind, my speech would have felt no caution and no anxiety that I might seem, in what I said, to fall short of what the subject deserves.

But now I am to speak of what is most godlike in him, the part of him that is akin to God: shut up in this visible and mortal frame, yet striving with all its labor to be made like God. As I call this to mind, I am about to touch in some way on greater matters, and through it on a kind of thanksgiving to God, because it has been granted me to meet such a man, beyond all human expectation, both that of others and my own. I had never proposed it, nor even hoped for it. Now that I am about to touch on such things, small as I am and wholly without understanding, I shrink back, not without reason, and hesitate, and would willingly keep silent.
translator_notes: The print reads οὐκ εὐλόγως (literally 'not reasonably'), which contradicts the argument. The Vossius Latin column has 'non immerito subterfugio ac formido' ('not without reason I shrink and fear'), and 2.2 goes on to call silence safe, so the English follows 'not without reason'. 'εἶτα μέλλω καὶ ἀναβάλλομαι' is rendered 'and so hang back and delay': it is not such small themes that make him hesitate; for them his scruple would be excessive. The print 'οὐκ εὐλόγως' was checked on the page image (PDF 75, Greek col. A); the Latin column there reads 'non immeritò cunctor ac timeo, & silere prorsus malo'. 'Shut up in this visible and mortal frame' supplies 'frame' for the bare neuter τῷ φαινομένῳ καὶ θνητῷ τῷδε (the body). 'Thanksgiving to God' renders εἰς τὸ θεῖον ('to the divine'). Possible echo of being 'made like God' (Plato, Theaetetus 176b, ὁμοίωσις θεῷ); not Scripture, not cited.
orientation: Gregory says he has come to praise not Origen's birth or body but the godlike part of the man, and so he shrinks from the task.

title: Afraid to walk into sacred hearing with unwashed feet
english: And so it seems safe to keep quiet. Otherwise, on the pretext of giving thanks but in truth perhaps out of rashness, I might say undignified, cheap and trite things about solemn and holy matters, and not only fail to reach the truth, but even, as far as lies in me, take something away from them in the minds of those who believe these things are so. For a weak speech will sketch them by insulting them rather than by matching the deeds in power. And yet what is yours, dear friend, cannot be torn down or insulted; and much more do divine things remain as they are, unshaken, not harmed at all by our small and unworthy words. But I do not know how we shall escape a name for boldness and rashness, having leapt in our folly, with small mind and small preparation, upon great matters, perhaps beyond us.

If we had been eager to show off like this elsewhere and before other people, we would have been bold even so, and somewhat at fault. Yet the rashness would not have been put down to shamelessness, since the bold venture would not have been made in your presence. Now, however, we shall fill up the whole measure of folly, or have filled it already, for we have dared to step, as the saying goes, with unwashed feet into ears where the divine Word himself makes his home. He does not walk there as he walks in the ears of most people, with his feet covered, as it were, by thick hides of riddling and obscure words. He walks there with bare feet, so to speak, clear and plain. And we, carrying our human words like filth or mud, have dared to pour them into ears trained to hear divine and pure voices.

Is it enough, then, to have gone wrong this far? Must we now at least begin to be sensible, and go no further with the speech, but stop here? I would like to. Yet since I have once been bold, let me be allowed first to state the cause that led me into this contest, in the hope that I may be pardoned for this rashness.
translator_notes: The print 'οὐ μὴν ἀλλ᾽ ἀναίδεια τῆς προπετείας αἰτία, τῷ μὴ ἐπὶ σοὶ ταῦτα θρασύνεσθαι' does not construe well. The English follows the sense of the Vossius Latin column ('sed tamen impudentiae tribuenda temeritas ... quod non coram te talia auderemus', partly lost in the scan): the rashness would not count as shamelessness, because it would not be ventured in Origen's presence; this also fits the contrast with 'νυνὶ δέ' ('Now, however'). Doubtful reading. 'With unwashed feet' (ἀνίπτοις τοῖς ποσί) is marked by Gregory himself as a proverb ('as the saying goes'; Latin margin 'Proverb.'), not Scripture. The bare feet of the Word may recall Exodus 3:5, but the image is Gregory's own; not cited. ὁ θεῖος λόγος is capitalized as 'the divine Word' since Gregory speaks of the Word dwelling in Origen's hearing. 'Dear friend' renders ὦ φίλη κεφαλή ('dear head'), a Greek idiom of affection; 'what is yours' renders the bare τὰ σά (Latin 'tua quidem omnia'). The Latin column for the doubtful clause was checked on the page image (PDF 75): 'tamen impudentiae tribuenda temeritas non esset, quòd non coram te talia auderemus'.
orientation: Gregory fears that a weak speech would insult holy things, yet resolves to explain why he has dared to speak.

title: Ingratitude is terrible; even the poor must give what they can
english: Ingratitude seems to me a terrible thing, terrible, indeed utterly terrible. For when someone has been treated well and does not even try to repay it, if in no other way, then at least with thanks spoken in words, he is either wholly senseless and unaware of the kindness done him, or forgetful. And if someone did at first perceive and recognize the good he received, yet memory does not keep it into the time that follows, and he does not render some thanks to the author of those good things, he is idle, ungrateful and impious, and his offense is unpardonable, whether he is great or small. If he is great and great-minded, it is unpardonable not to have his benefactor's great kindnesses on his lips with all thanksgiving and honor. If he is small and of no account, it is unpardonable not to sing the praises, and speak well, with all his strength, of the one who has done him good not only in great things but in small things too.

Those who are greater and stand above others in strength of soul must, as from a larger surplus and great wealth, render to their benefactors greater and more generous praises, as far as their power allows. Yet the small and those in straitened circumstances in their turn ought not to neglect this or grow careless, nor give up, as if they could bring nothing worthy or complete. Like people who are poor but grateful, they should measure not the power of the one honored but their own, and bring their honors out of the power they have. These will perhaps prove pleasing and welcome to the one honored, and with him they will not stand second to great and many gifts, if they are offered with greater eagerness and a whole heart. So it is recorded in the sacred books that a small and poor woman, among the rich and powerful who were offering great and costly gifts from their wealth, contributed small things, the very least, yet all that she had, and she alone carried off the testimony of having given more (Mark 12:41–44; Luke 21:1–4). For I think the sacred word did not weigh generosity and magnificence by the amount of the material given, which is outside a person, but by the intention of the one offering it, or rather by the choice.

So neither ought we to shrink back altogether because our thanksgiving will not equal the benefits. Quite the opposite: we ought to dare and to try, and to offer by way of return, if not equal honors, then at least the honors we can, in the hope that, even if our speech fails to give complete thanks, it may at least give partial thanks, and escape the name of utter ingratitude.

translator_notes: Clear allusion to the poor widow's offering; the wording 'πάντα ... τὰ ὄντα αὐτῇ' answers Mark 12:44 ('all she had') and Luke 21:4, so both Gospel passages are cited. The print's abbreviations near the end are expanded as 'τὴν εὐχαριστίαν ταῖς εὐεργεσίαις' (doubtful expansion of two τ-ligatures); the sense 'our thanksgiving will not equal the benefits' does not depend on the exact case endings. In the second sentence the predicate 'unpardonable' is supplied twice from the preceding 'οὐ συγγνωστά', which governs both infinitive clauses ('not to carry on his lips', 'not to sing the praises'). 'Did at first perceive' keeps πρῶτον with προσεγένετο. 'She alone carried off the testimony' attaches μόνη to ἀπηνέγκατο. 'A whole heart' renders γνώμῃ ὁλοκλήρῳ ('whole mind, entire intent').
orientation: Ingratitude is a terrible thing, so even one who can give little must offer what thanks he can.

title: No one can thank God as he deserves
english: For total silence is truly useless, hiding behind the plausible excuse of being unable to say anything worthy, while the attempt to make some return is always the mark of a grateful mind, even if the power of the one returning the favor falls short of what is deserved. For I will not keep silent because I cannot speak as the subject deserves. Rather, if I fulfill all that is in my power, I shall even take pride in it.

Let this speech of mine, then, be a thank-offering. I would not presume to say that it is offered to the God of the universe, although it is from him that all the beginnings of good things come to us, and it is with him too that we ought to begin our thanksgivings, hymns and praises. But even if I offered my whole self, not as I am now, profane and impure, mixed and soiled with a foul and unclean evil, but my very self laid bare, as pure, bright and clean as could be, unmixed with anything worse; even if, I say, I brought and gave my whole self bare, as though I were newly born, I could still bring no gift of my own worthy to honor and repay the Ruler and Cause of all. No one could ever praise him worthily, neither each person on his own, nor all together, not even if all things became, as it were, one and the same, all pure, going out of themselves and turning instead to him, gathered in one spirit and with one impulse, in harmony.

For even if any of his creatures could think of him in the best and fullest way, and could, if it may be said, speak of him as he deserves, still, for that very power, which he has been granted, receiving it not from anyone else but from him, there is no way he could find anything greater anywhere to offer in thanks.
translator_notes: 'παναγεῖ' as printed normally means 'all-holy', which cannot stand beside ἀκαθάρτῳ κακῷ; the English takes the sense 'foul', following the Vossius Latin column 'tetro atque immundo malo' (checked on the page image, PDF 77). Doubtful reading. 'ὥσπερ τινὰ γινόμενον' (as printed) is rendered 'as though I were newly born', following the Latin column 'nudum me velut recens natum offeram' (page image checked). The last sentence's opening 'ὅτι' is read as ὅ,τι ('whatever [creature]'), giving 'even if any of his creatures'. 'I would not presume to say that it is offered to the God of the universe' keeps the negation of 'οὐκ ἂν ἐθελήσαιμι λέγειν': Gregory declines to call his speech a thank-offering to God himself (he gives that task to the Word in 4.1). 'In one spirit' (ἑνὶ πνεύματι) means unanimity, not the Holy Spirit; lower case kept. Possible echo of Philippians 1:27 ('in one spirit'), too loose to cite.
orientation: Silence helps no one; Gregory will give what thanks he can, knowing that no one can thank God worthily.

title: Only the Word can give the Father worthy thanks
english: But the praises and hymns due to the King and Guardian of all, the unfailing fountain of all good things, we shall leave to him who heals our weakness even in this, and who alone can supply what is lacking: to the Protector and Savior of our souls, his firstborn Word, the Maker and Governor of all. He alone can send up to the Father unceasing and uninterrupted thanksgivings, both for himself and for all, for each one separately and for all together at once. For he is himself the Truth (John 14:6), and the Wisdom and Power of the very Father of all (1 Corinthians 1:24). Moreover, he is in the Father and wholly united to him, so there is no way that through forgetfulness, or lack of wisdom, or some weakness, as though he were a stranger to him, he should either fail to reach the Father's power with his own power, or reach it and yet willingly (which it is not lawful even to say) leave the Father unpraised.

He alone is able to fulfill most perfectly the full worth of the praises due to the Father. The Father of all himself has made him one with himself, and through him all but encompasses himself; honoring him in a way with a power equal in every respect to his own, he is himself honored. This, first and alone of all beings, his Only-begotten was given to have: God the Word who is in him (John 1:1). All others can be thankful and godly only in this way: if we ascribe to him alone, in return for all the good things we have from the Father, the power of worthy thanksgiving, confessing that this is the one way of godliness, that every remembrance of the Cause of all is made through him.

Therefore, for the unceasing providence over all things, which cares for us in the greatest things and in the least, and which has come even this far, let it be confessed that he is the worthy and unceasing Word of thanksgivings and hymns; for he is most perfect and living, the animate Word of the First Mind himself.

'His Only-begotten ... God the Word' may also echo John 1:18 (μονογενὴς θεός), and 'in him' John 10:38 or 14:10; left uncited as not certain. 'Protector and Savior of our souls' resembles 1 Peter 2:25 ('Shepherd and Overseer of your souls') but uses different words; not cited. 'Firstborn Word' renders πρωτογενὴς λόγος (not πρωτότοκος of Colossians 1:15); not cited. Agency kept in 'honoring him ... he is himself honored' (τιμῶν καὶ τιμᾶται): the Father honors the Son and is honored through him. 'All but encompasses himself' renders μονονουχὶ αὐτὸς αὐτὸν ἐκπεριιών literally; the Father, through the Son, as it were returns upon himself in praise. 'Through him' at the end of the second paragraph renders 'τὴν δι᾽ αὐτοῦ πᾶσαν μνήμην τῷ τῶν ὅλων αἰτίῳ'. In the last sentence λόγος plays on 'Word' and 'speech of thanks'; 'animate Word' renders λόγος ἔμψυχος ('ensouled Word') and 'First Mind' renders πρῶτος νοῦς, Gregory's philosophical name for the Father. orientation: Gregory leaves the praise owed to the King of all to the Word, who alone can give the Father worthy thanks.

title: The guardian angel who has led him from childhood
english: But let this speech of ours be a thank-offering, among all people, most of all to this holy man. And if I should wish to speak still more boldly, let it also be thanks to one of those beings who are not seen but are more divine, and who care for human beings: to him who, by some great judgment, was given charge of me from childhood, to manage, nurse and guard me, the holy angel of God, “who has fed me from my youth” (Genesis 48:15–16), as that man who was dear to God says, meaning, of course, his own.

He, being great, had a correspondingly great guardian: whether some other, whoever that may be, or perhaps the Angel of Great Counsel himself (Isaiah 9:6), the common Savior of all, whom, by reason of his perfection, he had by then received as his only guardian. This I do not know clearly. In any case, he knew and praised his own great one, whoever he may be. We, besides the common Governor of all people, acknowledge and praise also this one, whoever he is, who has been our own tutor from infancy. In everything else he has been in every way my good nurse and guardian, not as seems beneficial to me or to any of the friends close to me, for we are blind and see nothing of what lies ahead, so as to be able to judge anything of what is needed, but as seems beneficial to him, who foresees everything that helps our soul. Long ago and still now he nurtures me and leads me by the hand.

And besides all this, he contrived to join me to this man, the most important thing of all. I was not related to him by family or human blood, nor connected in any other way, nor one of his neighbors, nor even of the same nation at all, the very things that give most people their grounds for friendship and union. To put it shortly, we were unknown to each other, strangers, foreign to each other, standing very far apart, as far as the nations, mountains and rivers in between could separate us. Yet he brought us together by a providence truly divine and wise, and contrived this saving meeting for me, foreseeing it from above, I think, from my first birth and upbringing. How he did so would take long to recount, not only for one who speaks with precision and tries to leave nothing out, but even if I were to pass over most of it and chose to recall, in brief, a few of the most important points.
