translator_notes: Psalm numbering: 'speak the works of men' answers Psalm 16:4 in the LXX ('that my mouth may not speak the works of men'), Psalm 17:4 in English Bibles; the Babylon passage follows LXX Psalm 136:1-4, English Psalm 137:1-4 (captors asking for songs is 137:3). 'Paradise of delight' (παράδεισος τρυφῆς) is the LXX name for Eden (Genesis 3:23-24); the expulsion is cited once at 'a second Adam out of paradise'. 'Eat earth all the days of my life' uses the wording God speaks to the serpent in LXX Genesis 3:14 (γῆν φάγῃ πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ζωῆς σου) but is applied to Adam's sentence, where 3:17 has 'in sorrows you shall eat of it all the days of your life' (Gregory's next word is λύπας, griefs); cited as Genesis 3:17, with 3:14 noted here. 'Work the earth' (3:23) is present tense in the Greek (ἐργάζομαι) beside the future ἔδομαι; the English keeps the present. The reversal of Abraham's call (land, kindred, father's house) is cited as Genesis 12:1. Left uncited as uncertain: 'the ancient deception' (the serpent's deceit, Genesis 3:13, no shared wording beyond ἀπάτη); 'turning back toward what lies behind' (τὰ ὀπίσω; Luke 9:62 or Philippians 3:13 possible); 'by day and night' (Psalm 1:2 possible); 'work in clay' (Israel's bondage, Exodus 1:14, possible); forgetting (Psalm 137:5 possible). Ambiguities: 'the house of him who is truly our father' most naturally means Origen as spiritual father, whose house is the school Gregory is leaving (the prodigal comparison then says 'we leave the good things with you'); it could be read of God, so 'father' is kept lower case and not capitalized. 'The penalties of the ancient wrongs' renders τῶν ἀρχαίων δίκαι, where τῶν ἀρχαίων may be neuter (ancient deeds) or masculine (the first parents). 'τῶν δὴ' after ἐξέρχομαι is read as 'from these things' (the print's τ-compendium; τὸ δὴ possible). 'μηδ᾽ ἀξιουμένους ὑπὸ τῶν κρατούντων' is taken as 'even when their masters asked them', matching Psalm 137:3. 'κατακωχή' (print; marginal ἴσ. κατοχή not adopted) is rendered 'inspiration of God holds us', the Platonic sense of being possessed by a god. The last paragraph's opening 'Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἀπιών, ἄκων μόνον ὥσπερ αἰχμάλωτος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἑκὼν ἄπειμι' is elliptical; it is read as an unfinished wish ('if only I went merely unwillingly ... but I go willingly too'), as the facing Latin of the Paris 1622 print takes it ('Quod si abiens, inuitus abirem, ut captiui solent: at volens abeo'). ἐκπεπολεμημένος ('warred out') is rendered 'driven out ... by my own warfare against myself'. χλιδή is rendered 'luxury' (Latin 'deliciae'). The nominative ὑπομιμνησκόμενοι after the generic accusative μένοντας is taken as first person ('we can only weep ... as we remember'). 'ἐμάνθανον σιωπῶν, ἀλλὰ μὴ ... ποιήσασθαι': the negative infinitive is taken under the preceding ὄφελον ('If only I had not put on this novel spectacle'). 'Eat earth all the days of my life' is cited as Genesis 3:17 with the Genesis 3:14 wording noted above.
orientation: Leaving Origen's school, Gregory compares himself to Adam driven from paradise, to the prodigal son and to the exiles in Babylon.

title: Comfort: the Savior keeps watch, and the seed goes with us
english: But why do I lament like this? There is the Savior of all, the guardian and physician of all who are half dead and all who have been robbed (Luke 10:30–34): the Word who never sleeps, the keeper of all people. We have seeds too: those you showed us we already had, and those we have received from you, your good counsels; with these we go. We go weeping, as people setting out on a journey, yet carrying these seeds with us all the same (Psalm 126:6). Perhaps, then, the Keeper will stand over us and bring us safely through; and perhaps we shall return to you again, bringing from the seeds both the fruits and the sheaves (Psalm 126:6). They will not be perfect; how could they be? They will be such as we are able to bring from the business of public life: spoiled, it is true, by some power that is barren or bears bad fruit, yet a power that, if God consents, will not be ruined further along with us.

translator_notes: Psalm numbering: going out weeping with seed and returning with sheaves is LXX Psalm 125:6 (πορευόμενοι ἐπορεύοντο καὶ ἔκλαιον βάλλοντες τὰ σπέρματα ... αἴροντες τὰ δράγματα αὐτῶν), English Psalm 126:6; cited at both the weeping and the sheaves. 'The half dead and the robbed' continues the image of the man who fell among robbers (Luke 10:30-34), whose helper tends and heals him. Left uncited as uncertain: 'the Word who never sleeps, the keeper' may echo Psalm 121:4 (LXX 120:4, 'the one who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep'), but the wording differs (ἄγρυπνος, φύλαξ); 'the Savior of all' may echo 1 Timothy 4:10. 'Word' and 'Savior' are capitalized as Christ; 'the Keeper' is capitalized where it names him as a title. 'δραγμίδας' as printed (sheaves; the LXX has δράγματα). The first ἢ before ἀκάρπῳ has unusual breathing marks in the print and is read as ἢ ... ἢ. The last clause is compressed: the feminine datives (τῇ δυνάμει ... τινί ... προσδιαφθαρησομένῃ) agree, so it is 'the power', not the sheaves, that will not be ruined further; the English keeps that construction. The power may be the corrupting force of public business or Gregory's own capacity; the English leaves it open. The facing Latin of the Paris 1622 print takes the last clause the same way ('corruptos quidem facultate vel infrugifera, vel malae alicuius frugis; sed non amplius apud nos corrumpenda, si Deus annuerit').
orientation: Gregory takes comfort: the Savior of all keeps watch, and the seeds Origen sowed go with him.

title: Ending the speech: thanks spoken plainly
english: So let my speech end here. It has been bold where it least ought to have been; but it has given thanks in some fashion, I think, with a grateful mind and as far as we are able. We have said nothing worthy, yet we have not been wholly silent. It has also wept its farewell, as those who part from their friends usually do. Whether it has nothing boyish or flattering in it, nothing old-fashioned or overdone, I cannot say. But this I know clearly: it has this much, that it is not made up. It is true in every way, from a sound mind and from a purpose that is sincere and whole.
translator_notes: No Scripture. Doubtful reading: the word after μειρακιῶδες is a compendium read as μηδὲ; μὲν ἢ is possible. Either way the clause ends with 'οὐκ οἶδα' (I do not know), so the English puts it as an open question, 'Whether it has nothing boyish or flattering in it, nothing old-fashioned or overworked, I cannot say', which fits both readings and makes no claim either way. The genitive plurals 'λεγόντων ... σιωπησάντων' (as printed) shift from the speech to the speakers ('we'); the English follows that shift. 'ἐφ᾽ οὗ ἥκιστα ἐχρῆν' as printed: 'where it least ought to have been' (bold toward the very teacher before whom boldness was least fitting). 'Wept its farewell' renders ἀποκλαυσάμενος. προαίρεσις is rendered 'purpose' (deliberate choice). 'οἷα οἱ ἀποδημοῦντες τῶν φίλων εἰώθασι' is rendered 'as those who part from their friends usually do' (facing Latin 'sicut qui ab amicis digrediuntur, facere solent'). The facing Latin also reads the doubtful clause as an open question ('An puerile nihil, vel adulatorium; nihilve obsoletum, vel superfluum habeat, nescio'), supporting the English.
orientation: Gregory ends his speech, sure that its thanks, though unworthy, are sincere.

title: Farewell prayer: send us off under God's care
english: But you, my dear friend, rise and pray, and now send us on our way. As you saved us while we were with you by your sacred teachings, save us by your prayers once we have gone away. Hand us over and commit us; or rather, hand us over to the God who led us to you. Give him thanks for what he has already done for us, and ask him to lead us by the hand in what is to come as well: to stand over us always, to whisper his commands to our minds, and to instill in us his divine fear, which will be the best of tutors. For once we have gone away, it will not be in the freedom we had with you that we obey him. Ask him also that some comfort may come to us from him for our parting from you: that he send a good escort, an angel to travel with us. And ask, too, that he turn us back and bring us to you again. This above all, and this alone, will comfort us.
translator_notes: No Scripture is quoted. Left uncited as uncertain: the 'fellow-traveler angel' may echo Raphael in Tobit 5; 'commit us' (παρατίθεσο) may echo Acts 20:32 ('I commend you to God'); 'tutor' (παιδαγωγός) may echo Galatians 3:24. 'ὦ φίλη κεφαλή' (literally 'O dear head', a Homeric form of address) is rendered 'my dear friend'. 'εὐχαριστῶν ... ἐπὶ τοῖς φθάνουσιν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν' may mean thanking God on our behalf or for his past favors to us; 'give him thanks for what he has already done for us' keeps both. Pronouns for God are lower case, matching the rest of this book. Doubtful reading: 'ἐμβάλλοντα' (present) has an unclear ligature; ἐμβαλόντα (aorist) is possible and does not change the sense. 'οὐ γὰρ ἐν τῇ μετὰ σοῦ ἐλευθερίᾳ, καὶ ἀπελθόντες ὑπακουσόμεθα αὐτῷ': the negative governs the phrase 'in the freedom with you', not the obeying itself (facing Latin 'non enim eadem qua apud te libertate, etiam digressi, obediemus illi'); the English word order makes that scope explicit. ἀπόλειψις is rendered 'our parting from you'. ὑπηχοῦντα is rendered 'whisper' (sound in the mind). This is the end of the oration.
orientation: Gregory asks Origen to pray for him and to commit him to the care of God, who led him there.
